hints: Focus on what temperature actually changes, the speed of the particles or the energy levels of reactants and products?
Remember that $E_A$ is the energy gap from reactants to the top of the hump, so ask yourself if heating changes that gap.
Link faster successful collisions to the concentration-time curve, a faster reaction must make the reactant fall more steeply at the start.
walkthrough:
**What temperature does to the pathway**

Think of the enthalpy profile as a map of energy levels. Heating gives particles more kinetic energy, but it does not change the enthalpy of reactants, products or the transition state.

So the rule is:
$$E_A \text{ (with higher T) } = E_A \text{ (original)}$$

**What temperature does to the rate**

Higher temperature means more frequent collisions and many more particles with energy $\ge E_A$. The reaction gets faster.

Faster means reactant is used up more quickly at the start.

**Apply to the two diagrams**

Diagram 1 (enthalpy vs progress) must look identical, same starting level, same peak height, same finishing level. Diagram 2 (concentration vs time) must start at the same concentration but fall more steeply and flatten earlier.

Only one pair shows unchanged $E_A$ plus a steeper concentration drop.

options.A: Diagram 1 is correct because $E_A$ is unchanged, but Diagram 2 is identical to the original. Higher temperature must increase rate, so concentration should fall more steeply. This option misses the kinetic effect.
options.B: Diagram 2 correctly shows a faster fall, but Diagram 1 wrongly shows a taller hump with larger $E_A$. Temperature does not increase activation energy, that is a common confusion with the Boltzmann distribution where more particles overcome the same $E_A$.
options.C: Perfect match. Diagram 1 is unchanged so $E_A$, $\Delta H$ and energy levels stay the same. Diagram 2 starts at the same initial concentration but drops much more steeply, showing faster use of reactant due to increased temperature.
options.D: Both parts are wrong for increased temperature. Diagram 1 shows increased $E_A$ which never happens on heating (only a catalyst lowers $E_A$). Diagram 2 shows no change in rate, but rate must increase.
